WONDERLINE · LOD

Wonderline MUI Redesign

Full-cycle UX/UI discovery for the Loyalty-on-Demand management interface — grounding the Campaign & Offer Configuration redesign.
Client: Wonderline — Loyalty on Demand (LOD)
Scope: MUI redesign · Campaign / Offer Configuration wizard (free trial)
Users: Client-side marketing & customer-service teams (non-technical)
Trial start: 2026-09-16 · next call Wed 16 Sep, 14:00–15:00
Prepared by: Eleken — UX Research
00

The Brief in Plain Language

Read this first. No jargon. If you're new to the project, this is everything you need to know before the detail.

What is Wonderline?

Wonderline is a company (based in Hungary) that builds loyalty programs — the "collect points, get offers" systems behind big retail and fuel brands. Their product is called Loyalty on Demand (LOD). The headline client is Shell, whose loyalty program runs on LOD and covers about 9 million active customers.

The product has existed for roughly 20 years, but it was built as a bespoke, Shell-specific system. Wonderline now wants to sell it to the wider market — other fuel and retail brands — as a proper product. That means two things are happening at once: a rebranding of the company (handled by a separate branding partner) and a redesign of the software (that's us).

The thing we're actually redesigning: the "MUI"

Careful with this acronym — it is not Material UI. MUI = Management User Interface. It's the web-based admin console that a client's staff log into to run their loyalty program: set up campaigns and offers, look up customers, handle support cases, read analytics.

Two things matter about who uses it:

  1. The people using it are the client's staff, not Wonderline's — e.g. Shell's marketing and customer-service teams.
  2. Most of them are non-technical. Marketers who want to launch an offer without asking IT for help. The client's exact wish: "we want marketing people without IT support to use our product."

The customer-facing mobile apps are white-labeled (they carry the client's brand). The MUI is not — it stays under Wonderline's own brand. So the MUI is Wonderline's shop window: it's what prospects see in a demo.

What's wrong today

The client is refreshingly honest about it. The MUI "looks like 20 years ago," it's "very technical," and it's not built for marketers. There are around 50 sub-pages and an overwhelming left-hand menu. They have no in-house designer (they had one about a year ago; it didn't fit their Agile cadence). Their current "new" screens are a mix of team effort and AI-generated mockups they themselves call "really, really low level." The gap they feel most: a product that handles millions of customers and complex enterprise integrations, but an interface that doesn't look like it.

What we're designing for the trial

This is a free trial (Eleken's usual 3–5 day proof-of-value) to win a longer-term engagement. The agreed trial task is a redesign of the Campaign / Offer Configuration flow — one of their flagship demo features and one of the most-used, most-complex screens.

The flow is already a 5-step wizard: Target → Trigger → Validity → Benefit → Offer Details, with a live "Offer Summary" panel on the right that fills in as you go, and a "Go to Advanced Setup" escape hatch for genuinely complex offers. So the bones are there — the job is to make it feel modern, calm, and usable for a non-technical marketer, while keeping an advanced mode for power users setting up complicated Shell offers.

What "good" looks like

  • Modern and clear — looks like a credible, market-ready enterprise product, not a 20-year-old internal tool.
  • Usable by a non-technical marketer without IT support — plain language, sensible defaults, guidance, no wall of red validation errors.
  • Simple on the surface, powerful underneath — novices get a clean guided path; power users can still reach every advanced option.
  • On brand — red, black, gray, white; white-heavy; simple but signalling that it handles complexity at scale.
  • Demo-ready — good enough to put in front of prospects at the autumn conferences.

The boundaries

  • Keep the brand colours: red, black, dark gray, white. Interface should be white-dominant.
  • The MUI stays Wonderline-branded (not white-labeled per client).
  • Built in Java with a limited existing design system — heavy customisation costs dev effort, so be pragmatic.
  • Analytics run on Amazon QuickSight, which they can't change.
  • The tool runs behind their VPN, so we likely won't get hands-on access — we work from the walkthrough video + business-analyst documentation.
  • No explicit ask for gamification of the admin tool — don't add it.

The one thing that wins this project

Make the Campaign/Offer wizard feel effortless for a non-technical marketer — turning "very technical, looks 20 years old" into "simple, but clearly handles complex environments" — in a single, demo-ready flow. That is the exact promise the client is testing, on the exact screen they show prospects. Nail that and the trial converts.

  1. [23:53] Barbara Nyilas: "MUI, it's the management user interface." (Kills the Material-UI confusion — this is the admin app.)
  2. [24:00] Maksym Chervynskyi: "you're telling MUI, and I'm always like Material UI, Material UI." (The confusion, on record.)

02

Project Intelligence (Internal)

Sourced from Eleken's own Notion project page (⛽ Wonderline, "Projects planning" → last edited 2026-09-10) plus the discovery call. This is the account team's read of the deal — treat it as the internal source of truth for scope, success criteria, and the trial.

Deal snapshot

Field Value
Client Wonderline — product: Loyalty on Demand (LOD)
Company site lod.club/about-us
Location Hungary
Topic Loyalty program for oil & gas / fuel & retail
Engagement type Full-time (per Notion)
Type of work Redesign
Status Ready for designer
When ready to start ASAP
Trial start date 2026-09-16
Owner (Eleken) Kateryna Kruhlova (sales) + Maksym Chervynskyi (Head of Design)

What they need designed (per Notion)

"A web-based management interface (MUI) plus company rebranding, with later redesign work for the white-labeled customer mobile app. The main focus right now is the MUI on the web."

  • MUI redesign — primary, now.
  • Rebranding — in parallel, via a separate branding partner Eleken is introducing. Design work should align with it.
  • Customer mobile app — later, budget-dependent. Explicitly not the current focus.

Product maturity

Live ~20 years as a Shell-specific, highly customized solution. Now being productized + rebranded for external market use. Major parts of the UI are being actively (self-)redesigned already — some of what we see in the demo is brand-new, team/AI-built, and admittedly rough.

Timeline & commercial context

  • No hard deadline, but "start immediately" — they're preparing to go to market.
  • Short-term goal: something demo-ready by end of this year.
  • Conferences & networking events from October; some prospect meetings already scheduled. They know nothing we design will be production-ready by then, but they want a strong direction.
  • The first trial deliverable is expected within the usual 3–5 day free-trial window.
  • Next call: Wed 2026-09-16, 14:00–15:00 (client time) — the client's business analyst will join to explain the flow; the designer will present first screens.
  • They will also provide a screen recording of the campaign-config flow narrated by their analyst + documentation.

Pain points (Notion's framing, with the client's own quotes)

Business - Moving beyond Shell-only to market: "we decided that this is the time to go to the market with our product." - Looks outdated/too technical for enterprise demos → weakens positioning: "we really need to have the feeling of something that is simple, but still handling complex environments and systems." - No in-house UI/UX skill: "we have no professional for it, and I see that this is really taking us back."

User - Non-technical users struggle with the current MUI's complexity. (Notion notes a reaction of being "shocked" / "didn't even understand what's going on there.") - Overly complex screens & menus, esp. campaign config + customer management: "There are so many different thing that are…" (Alex, on the menu).

Design - Internal prototypes/screenshots too low quality, off the MUI: "these prototypes were really, really, low level."

Expectations (what a "win" includes for them)

  • A designer who makes it easier for non-technical users: "we want marketing people without IT support to use our product."
  • Rebranding + MUI redesign, not a narrow UI task: "I am looking for more, like, a rebranding… of the company and the MUI."
  • Help structuring their mixed ideas into a coherent product: "we need actually to structure all of those ideas into something more sufficient."
  • UX for both simple and advanced users: "…catering the software both… to more technical users who need more filters and less technical users who need everything to keep everything simple."
  • A longer-term relationship with an external partner, not an in-house hire.

Success criteria (Notion, verbatim intent)

Success = the redesign looks modern and clear, fits enterprise positioning, and presents Wonderline as a credible, market-ready product; the MUI is intuitive enough for non-technical marketers to operate without IT support; the result is usable for demos; and the trial shows a strong direction aligned with the coming rebrand. Anchor quote: "the product does not look like 20 years ago it looked like."

Constraints / tech limitations (Notion)

  • Keep brand colours: red, black, dark gray, white; prefer a simple, white-heavy interface.
  • MUI is not white-label — stays under Wonderline's brand. (Apps & website are white-label.)
  • Built in Java, many subpages (~50), limited design system → some customisations need extra dev effort.
  • Analytics run on Amazon QuickSight — cannot be changed.

The trial task (Notion, verbatim intent)

"A small but representative redesign of the campaign configuration flow — one of the main subpages used most often by non-technical users. The flow includes choosing customers or segments, selecting triggers, setting validity, defining benefits, and creating an offer. It should improve usability for both simpler and more advanced campaign setups while keeping complex cases available as an advanced mode, and test whether the designer can make a complex admin system more intuitive, modern, and aligned with Wonderline's branding."

Materials referenced on the Notion page: - Campaign-config demo video (Google Drive link) — this is the "Offer wizard demo" file in the folder. - 1st call (Attio Call Intelligence) + transcript (Google Docs). - 2nd call (Attio Call Intelligence) + transcript (Google Docs) — the "Transcript.txt" in the folder.

Key intel not obvious from the product itself

  • Barbara (CSO) is the buyer/champion but not the product expert. Finance→strategy background; repeatedly defers deep product questions to the business analysts. Design decisions that need domain truth must be verified with the analyst on the next call — don't assume from the UI alone.
  • The demo tool runs only via VPN → plan for no hands-on access; rely on the walkthrough + analyst recording + docs.
  • The demo already mixes two things: the real Java UAT tool (externaldemouat.lod.club) and separate AI-generated HTML mockups the analyst built (segment-breakdown modal, multi-condition builder). Their aspirations are visible in those mockups — useful signal, but they're unbuilt.
03

Personas, Pain Points & Journey

Prepared by: UX Research (Eleken) Scope: MUI (Management User Interface) redesign, anchored on the Campaign/Offer Configuration flow Evidence base: Discovery/sales call transcript (Eleken × Wonderline) + Eleken internal Notion product analysis Date: 2026-09-14

How to read this document

Every claim is tagged by evidence type:

  • [Verified — call] — stated directly in the transcript; verbatim quote + [timestamp] + speaker.
  • [Verified — Notion] — established project intel from the Eleken internal analysis.
  • (inferred) — a reasonable design/research conclusion drawn from the evidence, not stated outright. Flagged so it can be validated with the client (ideally in the next call with the business analyst present).

A recurring caveat: the transcript captures Wonderline staff describing their own tool and their clients' behavior, not the end-users (Shell marketers, customer-service agents) speaking for themselves. So user-side goals, thoughts, and frustrations are largely (inferred) from second-hand description until validated. This is the single biggest evidence gap — see "Research gaps" at the end.

1. Personas

Wonderline's MUI is used by their clients' staff (e.g. Shell), not by Wonderline itself:

"customer service also has access, for example, within Shell, they also have access to our MUI." — Barbara Nyilas [23:04] [Verified — call]

"The admin is used by their CLIENTS (e.g. Shell staff), not Wonderline's own staff." [Verified — Notion]

Access is role-based, and roles map to job function rather than a generic admin/viewer split:

"it's not about admin or just the viewer, it's more about, uh, the position or the role they have within the company, and this is how we set up access." — Barbara [26:20] [Verified — call]

That yields three personas below.

Persona 1 (PRIMARY) — "Marta," Non-Technical Marketing Manager at a client (e.g. Shell)

Attribute Detail

Primary JTBD "When I want to run a loyalty offer or campaign, help me configure and launch it correctly myself — without waiting on IT — so I can reach the right customers on time." (inferred, grounded in the flow below)

Frustrations with current MUI Looks dated; feels technical/engineered rather than marketer-friendly; overwhelming menu and nested sub-menus. (See quotes below.)
What "good" looks like "simple, but still handling complex environments" — modern, clean, intuitive enough to self-serve, and credible for enterprise demos. [Verified — call [14:18]; Notion success criteria]

"we really would like to have the feeling of ... something that is simple, but still handling complex environments and, and systems." — Barbara [14:18] [Verified — call]

Modern references named by the client: Comarch ("really modern design"), Eagle Eye, Loyalty Methods. — Alex [31:27]–[32:13], Barbara [33:44]–[34:07] [Verified — call]

Persona 3 (TERTIARY / POWER USER) — "The Shell Power User" (advanced-mode marketer / specialist)

Attribute Detail

Frustrations with current MUI The old paradigm was "all kind of filters you had to tick" — powerful but unfriendly. [Verified — call [9:12]]

"within Shell some of the offers are very complex ... and they have multiple rules ... We don't want to, um, have it, like, our main feature, but still we want to keep it as an advanced mode ... if anybody wants to go into details." — Barbara [48:16]–[48:48] [Verified — call]

Eleken confirms this is a known pattern: "we have lots of cases when we were catering the software both, like, to more technical users who need more filters and less technical users who need everything to ... keep everything simple." — Kateryna [48:50] [Verified — call]

Note: This may be a mode of Persona 1 rather than a separate person (the same marketer occasionally needs advanced control). (inferred) Worth validating with the business analyst.

2. Journey Map — Marketing Manager creates a campaign/offer today

Scope: the current campaign-config wizard as demoed. Flow stages confirmed in the call: Target → Trigger → Validity → Benefit → Offer Details → Create → Monitor. [Verified — call [15:39]–[16:36], [40:04]–[46:21]; Notion trial-task spec]

Note: "Thoughts" and most "Pain" cells are (inferred) — the end-user was not interviewed; they're grounded in the client's own descriptions of the tool and its audience.

Stage Actions Thoughts (inferred) Pain Opportunity
0. Log in / land Log into MUI (client VPN); arrive on dashboard/home. [Verified — call [35:21], [41:56]] "Where do I even start?" Menu is overwhelming; many top-level items + nested sub-menus. [Verified — call [37:16]–[37:37]] Simplify IA; surface a clear "Create campaign" entry point; reduce menu noise.
1. Find campaign config Navigate to Campaign Config via menu/sub-menu. [Verified — call [35:27], [36:09]] "Is this the right sub-page?" Deep sub-menus, "quite complicated." [Verified — call [37:23]] Flatten navigation; make the flagship flow easy to reach. [Flagship: call [19:58]]
2. Pick audience (Target) Choose all customers / a segment / dynamic segment; "Display segment" to preview. [Verified — call [40:04]–[41:23]] "Which segment? Who's actually in it?" Segment preview didn't render in demo ("It should" — bug/QA env). Dynamic segmentation still on roadmap → concepts in flux. [Verified — call [41:28]–[40:34]] Clear segment picker with a reliable, visible preview of who's included; accommodate dynamic segmentation.
3. Set Trigger Pick trigger (e.g. product purchase) or automatic/no-condition reward. [Verified — call [42:38]–[42:45]] "Does everyone get this, or only on an action?" Trigger logic isn't self-evident; needs mental model help. (inferred) Plain-language trigger choices ("Everyone" vs "When a customer does X").
4. Set Validity Set dates the campaign/offer runs. [Verified — call [43:11], [45:44]] "Is this the offer's dates or the price's dates?" Ambiguity confirmed: even the demoer/designer conflated validity-of-campaign vs validity-of-price. [Verified — call [45:55]–[46:18]] Unambiguous labels for what "validity" governs; separate concepts visibly.
5. Set Benefit Choose benefit: points, point multiplier, something free, etc. [Verified — call [43:16]–[44:18]] "What does 'point multiplier' actually do? Why an award role here?" Benefit mechanics unclear even to Wonderline's own staff on the call ("it's a good question," "we also don't know"). [Verified — call [44:28]–[44:37]] Inline explanations/examples for benefit types; clarify award-role vs earlier segmentation to avoid double-segmentation confusion. [Verified — call [44:44]–[45:06]]
6. Offer Details Add image, title, description. [Verified — call [45:34]] "Make it look right for customers." Comparatively straightforward; styling/consistency still weak overall. (inferred) Clean, previewable offer-detail step; show how it'll appear to end customers.
7. Create Click Create offer/campaign. [Verified — call [45:44]] "Did it work? What did I just launch?" No clear confirmation/summary described. (inferred) Pre-launch review/summary + confirmation state.
8. Monitor Open campaign list; view campaigns and "efficiency." [Verified — call [46:21]–[47:38]] "How is this campaign actually doing?" Per-campaign analytics not yet built ("that's a good question" re: how it's running; analytics module is a want). Confusing "test campaign vs campaign" labels nobody could explain. [Verified — call [46:21], [47:04]–[47:59]] Campaign analytics (charts/KPIs) surfaced in-context + on dashboard; clear naming/status taxonomy. [Verified — call [47:04]]

Environment caveat: Demo ran on a QA/DevFire test build over VPN, so some gaps (segment preview, a bug at [46:21]) are partly environment artifacts, not pure design defects. [Verified — call [41:33]–[41:42], [46:21]]

3. Prioritized Pain Points

Ranked; #1 is the clear priority.

🥇 #1 — HIGH — Campaign/Offer configuration is where complexity collides with non-technical users (and it's the flagship demo)

  • Pain: The multi-step campaign wizard mixes concepts non-technical marketers struggle with (segmentation, triggers, benefits, validity, award roles), several of which are ambiguous even to Wonderline's own team. It's simultaneously the flagship feature shown in demos and the chosen trial task.
  • Evidence:
  • Flagship: "campaign configuration, it's one of our, uh, flagship, uh, features." — Barbara [19:58] [Verified — call]
  • Trial task chosen: "I would say the campaign config here ... which is a really, really important part" / "Yeah. Let's, let's go with this one." — Alex & Barbara [39:40]–[39:53] [Verified — call]
  • Ambiguity in the flow itself: validity confusion [45:55]; "why do you need to select award role here?" "it's a good question" [44:28]–[44:37]; benefit mechanics unclear [44:28]. [Verified — call]
  • Audience is non-technical and tool is "very technical" [20:28]. [Verified — call/Notion]
  • Notion trial-task spec: redesign the wizard (Target→Trigger→Validity→Benefit→Offer Details), simple for novices + advanced mode. [Verified — Notion]
  • Design direction: Redesign the wizard around a plain-language mental model: clear step labels, contextual help/examples per step, disambiguated concepts (validity, award role, benefit types), a reliable segment preview, and a pre-launch summary. Keep the novice path short; push complexity into an opt-in advanced mode (see #4).

🥈 #2 — HIGH — Overwhelming navigation: menu overload + deep sub-menus

  • Pain: Many top-level menu items and complicated nested sub-menus make the whole MUI hard to navigate. ~50 sub-pages. [Verified — Notion: "~50 sub-pages, overwhelming menu"]
  • Evidence: "The menu here for sure ... so many different thing" [37:16]; "you have to access directly on this sub-menu, which is quite complicated ... so many different one here" [37:23]; "It can be a little bit overwhelming" [37:20]. [Verified — call]
  • Design direction: Restructure information architecture — group/prioritize by role and task, flatten sub-menus, and give the primary persona a fast path to high-value flows (campaign creation, campaign list).

🥉 #3 — HIGH — "Looks like 20 years ago" / too technical for marketers → hurts enterprise credibility in demos

  • Pain: Dated, engineered look undermines Wonderline's enterprise positioning (9M active customers, Shell) and demo effectiveness.
  • Evidence: should not "look like 20 years ago" [9:08]; "we look very technical ... for marketing" [20:28]; managing "9 million ... active customers ... this kind of page, I think it does not reflect this" [16:51]–[17:01]; internal AI mockups "really, really low level" [6:52] (echoes Notion). [Verified — call/Notion]
  • Design direction: Modern, clean visual system in brand colors (red/black/gray, mostly white), benchmarked to Comarch/Eagle Eye, that signals "simple but enterprise-grade." [Verified — call [14:08], [31:27]]

#4 — MED — No graceful path for complex (advanced) offers

  • Pain: Simple wizard can't express Shell's complex multi-rule offers; the old "tick all the filters" advanced setup is powerful but unfriendly, and they want to keep it without making it the default.
  • Evidence: "within Shell some of the offers are very complex ... multiple rules ... keep it as an advanced mode" [48:16]–[48:48]; old paradigm "all kind of filters you had to tick" [9:12]. [Verified — call]
  • Design direction: Two-tier UX — simple wizard by default, an opt-in advanced mode for power users; progressive disclosure so complexity never blocks novices.

#5 — MED — Weak customer-service surfaces (customer base, transactions, profile)

  • Pain: The customer lookup, transactions, and profile pages — the customer-service agent's whole world — are explicitly called out as "not good."
  • Evidence: customer base "really not good" [16:36]; transactions "also not good" [17:01]; profile "still not where I want to get" [17:01]–[17:48]. [Verified — call]
  • Design direction: Fast, scannable customer search + a clean, focused profile/transaction view tuned to the narrow customer-service task set. (Secondary to campaign work.)

#6 — MED — No per-campaign analytics; unclear campaign naming/status

  • Pain: Marketers can't clearly see how a campaign is performing in-app; analytics is a planned module. Labels like "test campaign vs campaign" confuse even staff.
  • Evidence: "how it's running, that's a good question" [46:21]; analytics module is a want, to feed the dashboard [47:04]; "difference between test campaign and campaign? ... we also don't know" [47:38]–[47:59]. [Verified — call]
  • Design direction: In-context campaign analytics (charts/KPIs) + dashboard rollup; a clear, documented naming/status taxonomy. (Partly a feature build, not pure redesign — flag scope.)

#7 — LOW — Dashboard still in flux

  • Pain: The home dashboard is mid-redesign; advanced analytics currently lives outside MUI in Amazon QuickSight.
  • Evidence: "We are actually doing a redesign for the full dashboard" [35:27]; advanced analytics "outside of MUI ... in Amazon QuickSight" [14:18]–[15:15]. [Verified — call/Notion]
  • Design direction: Align a clean dashboard (KPIs + campaign performance) with the new system; decide what to pull in from QuickSight vs link out. (Lower priority; already client-owned WIP.)

4. Design Principles (derived from the evidence)

  1. Simple by default, powerful on demand. Novice-first wizard; advanced mode via progressive disclosure. [from [48:34], [48:50]]
  2. Speak marketer, not engineer. Plain-language labels and inline explanations; strip technical framing that alienates non-technical users. [from [20:28]]
  3. Disambiguate every concept. No ambiguous terms (validity, award role, benefit types) — if Wonderline's own team stumbled on them, users will too. [from [44:28], [45:55]]
  4. Reduce navigational load. Flatten IA, role-based grouping, fast paths to high-value flows. [from [37:16]–[37:37]; Notion ~50 sub-pages]
  5. Enterprise-credible, modern, restrained. Clean, mostly-white UI in brand colors that signals scale (9M customers) and fits demos. [from [14:08], [16:51]]
  6. Design for demos as a first-class use case. The flagship flows must look and feel great when shown to prospects. [from [19:58], [9:08]]
  7. Show the outcome. Segment previews, pre-launch summaries, and in-context campaign performance so users trust what they're launching. [from [41:23], [46:21]]

5. Success Metrics (how we'd know the redesign worked)

Grounded in the client's stated success criteria ("modern/clear, enterprise positioning, intuitive for non-technical marketers WITHOUT IT support, usable for demos" [Verified — Notion]):

  • Self-serve completion: A non-technical marketer completes the full campaign-config flow end-to-end without IT/BA support and without misinterpreting any step (validity, benefit, award role). (Measure via moderated usability test / task-success rate.)
  • Time & steps to launch: Reduced time-to-create a standard campaign and fewer navigation detours vs the current MUI. (Task-time + click-path benchmark, before/after.)
  • Navigation findability: Users find campaign config and campaign list quickly without wandering sub-menus. (First-click / findability test.)
  • Comprehension: Users correctly explain what each step does (esp. validity, triggers, benefit types) — the ambiguity that tripped up staff is gone. (Comprehension probes in testing.)
  • Demo readiness: Sales (Alex) and strategy (Barbara) rate the redesigned flow as demo-ready and "enterprise-grade" — no longer "looks like 20 years ago." (Stakeholder sign-off; qualitative.)
  • Advanced-mode coexistence: Power users can still configure complex multi-rule Shell offers via advanced mode without complicating the novice path. (Task success for both personas on the same build.)
  • Trial acceptance (leading business signal): Positive client feedback on the trial screens → progression to a paid engagement and inclusion in end-of-year demos. [Verified — call [27:53], [52:00]]

Research gaps (validate before/at the next call)

  • No direct end-user voice. All user goals/thoughts/frustrations are second-hand from Wonderline staff. Confirm with the business analyst (joining next call) and, ideally, a real Shell marketer/CS agent. [Verified — call [45:11], [49:23]]
  • Role/permission documentation promised but not yet provided. [Verified — call [26:31]–[26:44]]
  • Campaign-config walkthrough recording + BA explanation to be supplied — will resolve validity/award-role/benefit ambiguities. [Verified — call [49:34]–[49:54]]
  • Tool access for the designer uncertain (VPN-only, QA build). Confirm whether hands-on access is possible. [Verified — call [41:42]–[42:23]]
  • Technical constraint: built in Java with a "limited design system"; customization = larger dev effort. Scope designs with this in mind. [Verified — call [28:45]–[29:04]; Notion]
04

Current App — Screen Inventory

From the "Offer wizard demo" walkthrough (2026-09-10, ~21 min, recorded by the client's analyst Bányai András). Screens captured and analysed frame-by-frame. Important distinction: the demo shows TWO things side by side — (a) the real product (the Java "LoD.Club MUI", running on the UAT/test environment externaldemouat.lod.club, shown in Edge) and (b) separate AI-generated HTML mockups the analyst built to illustrate aspirations (file:///…/dynamic-segment-mockup.html, shown in Chrome with LoD wiki/documentation tabs open). Both are captured below and clearly labelled — the gap between them is itself a finding.

App structure at a glance

  • URL pattern (real tool): externaldemouat.lod.club/lod-tool/app/offer-mgmt/light/1005/… — note the path segment /light/: there is already a "light" (simplified) mode distinct from the advanced setup.
  • Top bar: tab strip (browser-tab-style in-app tabs: "Campaign Config", "New Offer: <unnamed>"), a red "+ Feedback" button, user (WLUSABA1), locale flag, and LODUAT wordmark.
  • Left navigation (the "~50 subpages" problem, verbatim from the tool): a long, dense, single-level-feeling menu with expandable groups:
  • Members → Search Customer, Customer Compensation…
  • Transaction…
  • Rewards → Award Rule, Badges, Beacon Map, C/V Definitions, C/V Maintenance, Campaign Config, Catalog, Gamification, Gifts, Promotion Codes, Receipt Message, Tier, Transaction Limit, Validity Limitation, Invite-only rewards, Coupons and Vouchers, Goals
  • DataLab, Analytix&In…, Engagewave, Creative, Inspector, CFlow
  • Footer: TEST build tag, "Collapse".
  • Observation: ~18 items visible under Rewards alone, several using internal jargon ("C/V Definitions", "Beacon Map", "CFlow", "Engagewave"). This is the overwhelm the client and Alex both named.

The trial flow: Campaign / Offer Configuration wizard (REAL tool)

The offer builder is a 5-step horizontal stepper with a persistent live "Offer Summary" right-rail. Steps: Target → Trigger → Validity → Benefit → Offer Details. The bones of a good wizard are already here — the problems are visual/interaction polish, not information architecture.

Step 1 — Target (real_wizard_target.png)

  • Heading: "Choose your target audience for maximum impact."
  • Three big selectable cards: All customers / Customer segment / Dynamic segment.
  • Selecting Dynamic segment expands inline: "Select Dynamic Segment" (e.g. Purchase behavior) + a dependent dropdown + a red "Display Segment" button.
  • Offer Summary rail (Target / Trigger / Validity / Benefit) already populates with defaults.
  • Design observations: the selected card gets a heavy red border + pink fill — reads as an error state, not a selected state (red = danger everywhere is a core problem). No live audience count until you press "Display Segment" (a full stop in the flow). "Go to Advanced Setup" sits as a secondary button = the escape hatch to advanced mode.

Step 2 — Trigger (real_wizard_trigger_options.png, real_wizard_trigger_product.png)

  • Heading: "Define the customer action that triggers this offer."
  • Cards: Automatic reward ("without any condition") / Product purchase ("buys certain products by quantity or value").
  • Product purchase expands: Criteria (number stepper) + unit dropdown (piece(s)) + Product Group dropdown + a gear/settings icon.
  • Design observations: same red-border-as-selection issue; the gear icon is an unlabelled affordance; unit/criteria row is cramped.

Step 3 — Validity (real_wizard_validity.png)

  • Options for how long the offer runs: Forever / Date range / recurring (e.g. "every 15th day of the month"). Summary rail reflects "Validity: Forever" or a date range.

Step 4 — Benefit (real_wizard_benefit.png)

  • Heading: "Define what customers receive when they complete the action."
  • Cards: Bonus points ("Award fixed bonus points") / Product benefit ("Free products, discounts, or percentage off") / Point multiplier ("Boost points gained through chosen award rule").
  • Product benefit expands: Benefit Type = Free / Amount / Percentage (pill toggle) + Product Custom Groups dropdown (e.g. Bread) + gear icon.
  • Design observations: this is where the wizard is strongest conceptually (clear 3-way choice), but the pill toggle + dropdown + gear again crowd a single row. "Point multiplier" references an "award rule" — jargon a marketer won't know (open question for the analyst: why a second segmentation-like concept here).

Step 5 — Offer Details (real_wizard_offer_details.png)

  • Heading: "Configure how your offer appears to customers."
  • Fields: Offer Title (e.g. "Bread for 20, get 2"), Offer Image (upload/drop), Description with a rich-text toolbar and a "Generate with AI" button.
  • Primary action: red "+ Create Offer."
  • Design observations: AI description generation is a nice existing feature to keep/elevate. Title/description/image layout is serviceable; the summary rail now shows the full offer — a genuine strength to lean into.

The AI-generated aspiration mockups (NOT the real product)

These were built by the analyst (Chrome, local HTML) to show where they want to go. They're cleaner than the live tool and reveal the client's own instincts.

Multi-condition dynamic-segment builder (mockup_dynamic_segment_builder.png)

  • Same Target step, but the Dynamic segment card now supports multiple stacked conditions joined by "AND" chips: Purchase behaviour = High value customers at risk AND Customer age = 20–29 AND Points balance = Top charity segment, each row removable (−).
  • The Offer Summary rail lists all three conditions as bullets.
  • Takeaway: they want a real AND/OR audience-rule builder — this is the direction to formalise (see UX patterns file). Still uses the red-border-as-container styling.

Segment-breakdown modal (mockup_segment_breakdown.png)

  • A modal: "Purchase behaviour — segment breakdown" with a big headline "Total customers matching this segment type: 87,220" and a distribution table (Champions 8,420 / 9.7%, Loyal 12,630 / 14.5%, Potential followers, New, Promising, Customers needing attention, Sleeping, At risk, High value customers at risk 3,110 / 3.6% (highlighted), Hibernating, Lost, Miscellaneous) with mini distribution bars and share %.
  • Takeaway: they clearly want live reach/estimated-audience feedback — the single biggest UX upgrade for a segment builder. Bring this inline and live into the Target step rather than behind a "Display Segment" click/modal.

Cross-cutting design observations (feed the pain-point list)

  1. Red = everything. Selection, primary action, validation, and brand accent are all the same red → a selected card looks like an error. Needs a proper semantic colour system (brand red reserved for primary/CTA; a neutral/positive treatment for "selected"; red only for real errors).
  2. No live audience feedback in-flow. Reach count is gated behind "Display Segment" / a modal. Should be live and inline.
  3. Cramped expand-in-place rows. Criteria/unit/group/gear pile into one line; spacing is tight; the gear icons are unlabelled.
  4. Nav overload. ~18 Rewards items + 6 other groups, jargon-heavy ("C/V Definitions", "Engagewave", "CFlow"). Prime candidate for grouping/renaming in plain language.
  5. The IA is actually good. 5-step stepper + live summary + advanced escape hatch is a solid skeleton. The trial win is restyling + interaction polish + live feedback, not re-architecting.
  6. Two sources of truth. Real tool vs AI mockups diverge; part of our value is unifying them into one coherent, buildable system (mindful of Java + limited design system).

Screens referenced (in research/screens/): real_wizard_target.png, real_wizard_trigger_options.png, real_wizard_trigger_product.png, real_wizard_validity.png, real_wizard_benefit.png, real_wizard_offer_details.png, mockup_dynamic_segment_builder.png, mockup_segment_breakdown.png.

05

Competitors & Market

Research for Wonderline / Loyalty on Demand (LOD). Prepared for the MUI redesign (Campaign/Offer Configuration wizard). Evidence-led; claims are cited inline. Items that could not be verified are marked [UNVERIFIED].

1. Positioning overview — where LOD sits

LOD is an enterprise loyalty engine with an operations/integration heritage, currently powering Shell's ~9M-customer European program (per client brief — [UNVERIFIED against public sources]; not independently confirmable). Its natural competitive coordinates:

  • Segment: Enterprise / large-scale, multi-country programs. Not SMB, not Shopify-app tier.
  • Vertical strength: Fuel & convenience + broader retail. This is a genuinely distinct niche — fuel/c-store loyalty has its own mechanics (cents-per-gallon discounts, fuel↔store attachment, high transaction frequency, POS-heavy redemption) that most horizontal loyalty vendors treat as an afterthought. Major fuel brands run heavily custom stacks: Shell's US "Fuel Rewards" runs on PDI Technologies as tech provider (NACS, CSP Daily News); BP runs BPme Rewards (CSP/CSNews context).
  • Core strength: Operations depth, integration, and reliability at scale — the "handles complex environments" story — built on ~20 years of Java engineering.
  • Geography: Europe-based (Hungary), Europe-proven. This aligns it against Comarch (Poland) as the closest peer — a European enterprise loyalty vendor productizing similar territory.

The strategic tension the redesign must resolve: LOD's differentiation is operational/technical depth, but the buyers and daily users of the MUI are non-technical marketing and customer-service teams. The market's clear direction of travel is no-code, marketer-autonomy campaign building (Talon.One, Antavo, Loyalty Methods' RCX Nexus all lead with this). LOD's whitespace is to pair its operational strength with a genuinely simple campaign builder — a combination competitors mostly do not deliver together (the deep-ops incumbents tend to be complex to use; the simple-UX challengers tend to be lighter on operational/fuel depth).

3. Deep dives — Comarch, Eagle Eye, Loyalty Methods

Comarch (the client's aspirational "modern design" reference)

  • What the admin/campaign UI does: Campaign Management module covers customer targeting, an interactive marketing calendar, multi-stage campaign planning with task workflows, automated actions, budget tracking, and campaign testing. The workflow/task-list UI was enhanced with tooltips per task and a summary of finished/active/outstanding tasks (Comarch Campaign Mgmt, latest updates).
  • Design maturity — the nuance the client should hear: Despite being their "modern design" aspiration, third-party reviews are mixed. The consistent theme: powerful but complex, steep learning curve, "less intuitive for day-to-day use," best for large orgs with dedicated technical+marketing teams — with the caveat that the newest version is meaningfully more user-friendly (Capterra reviews). It is a Forrester Wave Strong Performer, Q4 2025 (PRNewswire).
  • Screenshots/UI: No clean public gallery of the current admin UI was found via search [UNVERIFIED]. Best route: request a Comarch demo, or pull marketing-page/product-tour imagery directly from comarch.com and their news posts.
  • What LOD can learn / must match: The marketing calendar + task-workflow model is a strong pattern for campaign orchestration. But Comarch's own weakness (complexity, learning curve) is exactly LOD's opening — the brief is "simple but handling complex environments," which is precisely where Comarch is judged to fall short. LOD should match Comarch's feature depth and visual polish while beating it on first-run intuitiveness for non-technical users.

Eagle Eye (the bigger, well-funded reference)

  • What it does: AIR platform positions as a single central hub for the full promotion lifecycle — issuance → redemption → analysis — across in-store POS, e-commerce, and mobile, plus omnichannel loyalty (points/tiered/subscription + gamification) and a digital wallet (Eagle Eye AIR).
  • Design maturity: Marketed on API-first, composable/MACH-style architecture and real-time scale (grocery clients). Public reviews of the admin UX specifically are thin [UNVERIFIED] — Eagle Eye's public story is architecture and scale, not UI screenshots.
  • What LOD can learn / must match: The "one hub, whole lifecycle" narrative and real-time omnichannel redemption are table stakes at this tier. LOD's fuel/POS heritage is directly comparable to Eagle Eye's grocery-POS strength; the differentiator to press is admin simplicity, since Eagle Eye doesn't foreground it.

Loyalty Methods (client says "very similar to us")

  • Why it's the closest analog: Explicitly founded to implement/integrate enterprise loyalty into complex, multi-vendor stacks — the same operations/integration DNA the client describes for LOD (Our story, integration model). ReactorCX is headless, event-native, API-first, "operates inside existing ecosystems rather than replace them," with real-time earn/burn, promotion mgmt, and audit trail; ~4.2B transactions/yr across retail, fuel, hospitality, financial services (Loyalty engine). Fuel is explicitly a named vertical — a direct overlap.
  • The critical UI signal: Their next-gen RCX Nexus is pitched as "a new interface that makes complex configurations simple, with AI agents embedded directly inside your actual work" — including an AI Promotion Architect that builds complete campaigns from a plain-language brief, and multi-LLM support (Claude/GPT-4o/Gemini/BYO) (Loyalty Methods home). This is the single most important competitive datapoint: the most similar competitor is betting its UX story on making complex config simple + AI-assisted campaign creation.
  • What LOD must match / can learn: LOD's campaign wizard (Target → Trigger → Validity → Benefit → Offer Details) is competing directly against "describe the campaign in plain language and we'll build it." LOD doesn't need AI to win, but the bar for reducing configuration effort is now very high. Design implications: strong defaults, progressive disclosure, plain-language summaries of each wizard step ("what this offer will do"), and templates/duplication so marketers aren't building from zero. An optional AI-assist or natural-language summary layer would keep pace without over-committing.

4. Positioning gap / whitespace — where LOD can differentiate

The market splits into two camps, and almost nobody owns the intersection:

  1. Deep-ops incumbents (Comarch, Eagle Eye, Capillary, Annex Cloud) — feature-rich, enterprise-grade, but reputationally complex to operate (Comarch's steep learning curve is the archetype).
  2. No-code challengers (Talon.One, Antavo) — beloved for marketer autonomy / code-free builders, but lighter on the deep operational + fuel/POS environment story.

LOD's whitespace = operational depth + genuinely simple campaign building, in fuel & retail. Concretely:

  • "Simple but handles complex environments" is not a slogan — it's the exact unoccupied position between camp 1 and camp 2. Comarch is complex-but-deep; Antavo is simple-but-lighter; LOD can be deep AND simple.
  • Fuel & convenience specialization is a real moat. Horizontal vendors treat fuel as generic retail; the incumbents in fuel (PDI, custom brand stacks) aren't productized SaaS with modern admin UX. LOD is both fuel-native and productizing.
  • Non-technical marketer + customer-service usability as a first-class design goal. The wizard's job is to let a marketer configure a genuinely complex offer (multi-condition triggers, validity windows, tiered benefits) without feeling the complexity — via progressive disclosure, sane defaults, live plain-language previews of the offer's effect, and reusable templates. This is where Eleken's redesign directly creates the differentiator the sales story needs.
  • Design language: red/black/gray/white + "simple" positions LOD to look cleaner and more decisive than Comarch's denser enterprise UI — a visible, demoable proof point of the "simple" promise.

Risk to flag: The most-similar competitor (Loyalty Methods) is moving toward AI-generated campaigns from plain-language briefs. LOD should at minimum design the wizard so a natural-language summary / assist layer can be added later without rework.

Enterprise loyalty pricing is overwhelmingly custom / volume-based / "talk to sales" — normal for this tier (Talon.One incentive engines).

06

UX Patterns & Inspiration

Project: Wonderline / Loyalty on Demand (LOD) — MUI redesign (B2B admin console, web) Hero flow: 5-step Campaign / Offer Configuration Wizard — Target → Trigger → Validity → Benefit → Offer Details, with a live "Offer Summary" right-rail and a "Go to Advanced Setup" escape hatch. Audience: mostly non-technical client-side marketing and customer-service staff; power users need an advanced mode. Brand cue: red / black / gray / white, white-heavy, "simple but handles complexity." Scope note: the brief does not ask to gamify the admin tool — nothing below proposes that.

This document names established UX patterns, says when each applies, cites reference tools, and maps every pattern to a specific LOD wizard step. Where a product's exact behaviour is cited it comes from a source link; anything not cited is a general, named pattern, not a claim about a specific product's current build.

1. Multi-step configuration wizard patterns (complex B2B tools)

1.1 Wizard vs. single-scroll form — pick the wizard here, deliberately

  • What it is. A wizard splits a long task into a few ordered screens; a single-scroll form shows every field at once. The wizard's underlying principle is progressive disclosure — presenting inputs in manageable chunks to reduce the perceived effort of the whole task (WeWeb).
  • When to use. Multi-step wins specifically for complex, conditional, longer-than-~7-field flows aimed at a qualified/expert-ish audience — exactly the LOD case; simple transactional forms do not need fragmentation (Numinam, alfdesigngroup). Conversion/completion lifts are real but only when tailored to context — don't cite the numbers as a promise, cite them as "this is the right structure for complex flows."
  • LOD mapping. Keep the 5-step wizard as the default path. Each step should carry 1–3 primary decisions, not a wall of fields (WeWeb). The Target step's multi-condition builder is the one place that can grow — contain it (see §2), don't let it bleed into the other four steps.

1.2 Progressive disclosure (the spine of the whole design)

  • What it is. An interaction pattern, popularised by Jakob Nielsen, that defers advanced or rarely-used options to a secondary layer, making the tool easier to learn and less error-prone; the canonical example is the Print dialog's "Advanced" button (IxDF, Interaction Design / Shopify). Sub-step progressive disclosure reveals smaller tasks gradually while managing underlying complexity (WeWeb).
  • When to use. Whenever a screen has a "most people want X, some people want X + a lot more" shape.
  • LOD mapping. Each step is a branch: choosing "All customers" shows nothing further; "Dynamic segment" reveals the condition builder. "Product benefit" reveals Free / Amount / Percentage sub-controls only after the benefit type is picked. This is the mechanism that lets the console stay simple for novices while still "handling complexity."

1.3 Live summary / preview rail (the Offer Summary right-rail)

  • What it is. A persistent side panel that fills in as the user makes choices, giving continuous feedback and a running "here's what you're building." Campaign builders commonly pair a working area with a right-side panel for settings/preview while the centre stays the canvas (Mailchimp preview docs; right-panel patterns in Monday Campaigns and HighLevel per search summary).
  • When to use. Multi-step flows where the object being built is abstract (an offer/campaign) and the user benefits from seeing it assemble.
  • LOD mapping. The Offer Summary rail should update on every field commit (not on a separate "Display Segment" click — that's the current anti-pattern, §5). Show a human sentence, e.g. "Customers aged 25–40 with >500 points get 2× points on fuel, Jan–Mar." Include the live reach count here (see §2.2). On the final step it doubles as the review-before-submit summary (WeWeb).

1.4 Stepper design

  • What it is. The visual progress indicator across the top (or side) of a wizard. Guidance: horizontal steppers suit flows where a step depends on the previous one; linear steppers force order, non-linear/editable steppers let users jump back to edit; keep labels short; don't nest steppers (Material Design steppers, MUI Stepper, Telerik guidelines).
  • When to use. Any wizard of ~3–8 steps; use dots/labels for few steps, a progress bar for many.
  • LOD mapping. 5 labelled, horizontal steps: Target · Trigger · Validity · Benefit · Details. Make completed steps clickable to edit (editable steps) so users can revise Target after reaching Benefit without losing work. Keep it linear-with-back — later steps can depend on earlier choices, but let users freely step backward. LOD already uses MUI, so its native Stepper is the honest baseline to restyle in brand colours.

1.5 Save-as-draft / resume

  • What it is. Persisting partial progress so a user can leave and return; steppers may show a transient "saved" confirmation after a step (Material Design). Auto-save is repeatedly called out as one of the execution details that make multi-step flows actually work (WeWeb).
  • When to use. Long/high-stakes B2B configuration where an interruption mid-flow is likely (a CS agent gets pulled away; marketing needs sign-off).
  • LOD mapping. Auto-save each step; expose an explicit "Save as draft" and a Drafts list. Never lose data on Back navigation.

1.6 Inline validation done RIGHT (vs. the current all-red-borders approach)

  • What it is. Validating a field as the user finishes it, not while they type. Baymard's testing: fields should not be prematurely validated; error messages should clear the moment input is corrected; and positive inline validation (a green "all good") reassures users (Baymard). Fire validation on blur (leaving the field), or after a short pause — never on every keystroke, and never turn everything red up front (LogRocket, Baymard).
  • When to use. Every form field, always.
  • LOD mapping. Replace the current "everything red on load" behaviour (§5) with: neutral fields by default → validate on blur / on step-advance → clear the error instantly on correction → show positive confirmation on the fields that matter (e.g. a valid date range, a non-empty title). Block step-advance with a single, specific message, not a sea of red borders.

1.7 Smart defaults

  • What it is. Pre-selecting the most common, safe choice so novices can move forward without a decision. Adaptive/sensible defaults are a core progressive-disclosure companion (tengbao).
  • LOD mapping. Default Target = "All customers"; Trigger = "Automatic reward"; Validity = "Forever"; Benefit = "Bonus points." A user who accepts every default reaches the Details step in seconds. Power users override.

1.8 Guided vs. expert modes

  • Covered in depth in §4 — the "Go to Advanced Setup" escape hatch is the LOD instance of this pattern.

2. Segment / audience rule-builder patterns

The Target step's "Dynamic segment with multi-condition AND builder" is a query builder. This is a mature, well-referenced pattern — copy the good versions rather than inventing one.

2.1 AND/OR logic with rule groups (chips / rows)

  • What it is. Conditions expressed as rows ("Age is between 25 and 40"), combined with a combinator (AND/OR), and nestable into groups for compound logic. Reference implementations expose exactly this: a recursive RuleGroup of Rules with an inline AND/OR combinator, optional drag-to-reorder, and a readable summary output (React Query Builder docs).
  • Reference tools.
  • Braze — stack filters with AND/OR logic, nest segments within segments, apply AND/OR across filter groups (Braze segments docs).
  • Iterable — query-builder interface stacking properties, events and behaviours with AND/OR; note it is weaker on true nested grouping, which is a known limitation to design around (MoEngage comparison).
  • Klaviyo — conditions as reusable building blocks that include/exclude audience slices; supports compound conditions like "Placed order in last 30 days AND viewed product X but NOT purchased" (Klaviyo segment conditions, getting started).
  • HubSpot — complex segments via a friendly UI reused across campaigns, workflows and ad audiences (Maestra comparison).
  • LOD mapping. The brief specifies AND-only, multi-condition (purchase behaviour, age, points balance). Keep the trial that simple: a stacked list of condition rows joined by a fixed "AND" label, each row = attribute · operator · value. Reserve OR / nested groups for Advanced mode (§4) — that keeps the novice view a flat, legible list and avoids Iterable's nesting-confusion trap. Use chips for committed conditions so a segment reads as scannable tokens.

2.2 Live count / estimated reach (fix the "no count until Display Segment" gap)

  • What it is. Showing the size of the matching audience as the user builds, so they get immediate feedback on whether the segment is too broad or empty. Klaviyo live-previews segment size while you work (Klaviyo segmentation feature). Braze shows an estimated size by querying a sample and extrapolating — and explicitly frames it as an estimate that can drift, which is the honest way to present a fast count on ~9M-customer data (Braze — Measure Segment Size).
  • When to use. Any audience builder — this is table-stakes for the category.
  • LOD mapping. This is LOD's single biggest builder fix. Put an estimated reach count in the Offer Summary rail that updates as conditions change (debounced), labelled "~X customers (estimated)." Remove the current requirement to click "Display Segment" to see any number. On 9M-scale data, use a sampled estimate like Braze and label it as such rather than blocking on an exact count.

2.3 Chips / tokens for committed values

  • What it is. Rendering selected conditions or values as removable chips, so a compound segment is scannable and each token is individually editable/removable.
  • LOD mapping. Each committed condition becomes a chip in the builder and appears as plain language in the summary rail. One-click remove on each chip.

3. Campaign / offer builder references worth stealing from

  • Wizard + preview split. Marketing-automation builders converge on a working area (steps/canvas) + right-side panel (settings/preview) layout (Mailchimp, Monday Campaigns / HighLevel right-panel pattern per search summary). LOD's Offer Summary rail is the right instinct — commit to it as the persistent preview surface.
  • Desktop/mobile preview toggle & test send. Tools let users preview desktop vs. mobile and send a test before launch (Mailchimp, MS Dynamics 365 preview). LOD mapping: on the Offer Details step, preview the AI-generated title/description/image as the customer would see it before publishing.
  • Segment reuse across campaigns. HubSpot's segments are built once and reused in campaigns, workflows and ad audiences (Maestra). LOD mapping: let a Dynamic Segment built in Target be named and saved for reuse — supports the existing "Customer segment" option and reduces rebuild effort.
  • Review-before-launch step. A summary/review step before final submission is a repeated best practice (WeWeb). LOD's step 5 + summary rail already serves this; make the rail's plain-language sentence the explicit "confirm this is right" moment.

4. Balancing SIMPLE + ADVANCED

The core requirement — simple for novices, advanced for power users — is the textbook progressive disclosure / tiered-controls problem.

  • Tiered controls (basic vs. advanced). Show basic settings to everyone; put a secondary level for experienced users behind an "Advanced" affordance; the Print dialog is the canonical model (IxDF, tengbao). Related building blocks: contextual reveal on demand, collapsible sections, expert modes + keyboard shortcuts, adaptive defaults, and persistence of the user's preference (tengbao).
  • When to use. When the same tool serves a novice majority and an expert minority with genuinely more complex needs — LOD exactly.
  • LOD mapping. 1. "Go to Advanced Setup" as the escape hatch, not the default. The 5-step wizard is the guided path; the complex Shell offers live behind one clearly-labelled door. Progressive complexity means the user opts into depth, never gets dropped into it. 2. In-wizard tiering. Within a step, keep advanced knobs (OR logic, nested groups in Target; recurring rules in Validity; point-multiplier fine-tuning in Benefit) collapsed under "Advanced options" so the default view stays 1–3 decisions. 3. Persist the choice. Remember whether a user tends to use advanced mode and default them accordingly on return (tengbao). 4. No dead ends. Advanced Setup should carry over everything already configured in the wizard, not force a restart.

5. Anti-patterns to avoid (including LOD's current issues)

  • Everything red on load. Pre-emptively rendering all fields in an error state violates the "don't prematurely validate" rule and trains users to ignore red (Baymard). Fix: neutral by default, validate on blur/advance, clear on correction, positive confirmation where it helps (§1.6).
  • No live reach count until "Display Segment." Forcing an explicit action to learn segment size removes the continuous feedback loop that Klaviyo and Braze treat as core (Klaviyo, Braze). Fix: live estimated reach in the summary rail (§2.2).
  • Dense ~50-item nav. A flat 50-item navigation buries the hero flow and overwhelms non-technical users; it's the opposite of progressive disclosure, which defers rarely-used destinations (IxDF). Fix: group into a few top-level areas, surface the campaign wizard as the primary action, demote admin/rarely-used items into secondary sections.
  • Technical jargon for non-technical users. Labels aimed at engineers raise cognitive load for marketing/CS staff. Fix: plain-language labels and a human-sentence summary; save technical terminology for Advanced mode.
  • Nesting steppers / over-fragmenting. Don't embed steppers within steppers or split a short section into extra steps (Material Design). Keep the Target condition builder inside the Target step, not as its own wizard.
  • Deep/ambiguous nesting in the segment builder. Iterable-style query builders get hard to reason about without clear grouping (MoEngage). Fix: flat AND-list for novices; nested groups only in Advanced.
  • Losing work on Back / no draft. Multi-step flows must preserve data on back-navigation and support resume (WeWeb).

6. Shortlist — patterns to steal for the trial, by wizard step

Step Steal this Reference / rationale
All steps (chrome) Horizontal, labelled, editable stepper (click a done step to revise); auto-save + "Save as draft"; live Offer Summary rail written as a plain-language sentence; inline validation on blur (neutral → error-on-leave → clear-on-fix → positive confirm). Material steppers, MUI Stepper, WeWeb, Baymard
1 · Target Smart default = "All customers." Dynamic segment = flat AND-list of condition chips (attribute · operator · value); live estimated reach in the rail, sampled + labelled "estimated," no "Display Segment" click. OR / nested groups behind Advanced. Klaviyo, Braze size & segments, React Query Builder
2 · Trigger Default = "Automatic reward"; "Product purchase w/ criteria" progressively discloses its criteria only when selected. IxDF progressive disclosure
3 · Validity Default = "Forever"; "Date range" and "Recurring" reveal their controls on demand; recurring rules = advanced-tier. tengbao progressive complexity
4 · Benefit Default = "Bonus points"; "Product benefit" reveals Free / Amount / Percentage sub-controls after type selection; point-multiplier fine-tuning collapsed under Advanced. Shopify progressive disclosure
5 · Offer Details Preview the AI title/description/image as the customer sees it (desktop/mobile) before publish; summary rail becomes the review-before-launch confirmation. Mailchimp preview, WeWeb review step
Escape hatch "Go to Advanced Setup" carries over all wizard state; opt-in depth; remember the user's mode preference. tengbao, IxDF

07

Brand & Visual Foundation

No formal brand guidelines file was provided. This foundation is derived from two sources: (1) the client's explicit statements on the call about colours and feel, and (2) the actual product UI observed in the walkthrough (the LODUAT tool). A rebrand is underway with a separate partner, so treat this as a working system to align with — not a locked spec. Flag anything you lock in for confirmation against the new brand.

What the client actually said

  • Palette: "our colors, which we would like to stick to… red and black and gray and white. Mostly to use white because it's a management interface." — Barbara [14:10].
  • Feel: "we really would like to have the feeling of something that is simple, but still handling complex environments and systems." — Barbara [14:18].
  • Trend read: "we see that the trend is to go, like, as simple as it can be." — Barbara.
  • Reference: Comarch — "really modern design" (Alex). (But note: Comarch's own admin UI is widely called complex — borrow the polish, not the density.)

Colour system (derived — verify hex against rebrand)

The live tool uses a saturated brand red as its everything-colour. The core brand-foundation move for the redesign is to split "brand red" from "semantic red" so a selected item never looks like an error.

Role Colour (approx, verify) Usage
Brand Red #E30613–#E11B22 (observed LOD red) Primary CTAs, active stepper node, logo, key accents. Use sparingly — it should punctuate, not fill.
Ink / Black #111114 Primary text, headings, dark UI.
Graphite #3A3A40 Secondary text, icons.
Slate / Muted #6B6B73 Tertiary text, captions, placeholder.
Hairline #E6E6EA Borders, dividers, table rules.
Surface #F6F6F8 App background / panels (the "white-heavy" base).
White #FFFFFF Cards, content surfaces — the dominant colour.
Selected (NEW) tinted neutral or a desaturated brand tint, e.g. #FCEBEC fill + #111 accent, OR a cool neutral Selection state for cards/toggles — must NOT read as error. This is the single most important addition.
Success #1E9E62 Confirmations, positive counts (e.g. live audience reach).
Warning #C8811A Cautions.
Error (semantic red) reserve a red distinct in weight/context from brand red Real validation errors only.

Guardrail: In the current tool, brand red = CTA = selection = validation = error. Assign red one primary job (CTA/active) and give selection and error their own unambiguous treatments. This alone will make the interface feel dramatically calmer and more "modern."

Typography (derived / recommended)

No brand typeface was specified. For a white-heavy enterprise management console, use a clean, highly legible sans with strong number legibility (tables, points, KPIs):

  • Recommended: a neutral grotesque — Inter or IBM Plex Sans (Plex also gives a mono for IDs/codes, and reads "engineered/enterprise"). Match whatever the rebrand selects; propose one if they have none.
  • Type scale (suggested): Display 28/32 · H1 22/28 · H2 18/24 · Body 14/20 · Small 13/18 · Caption 12/16. Dense-but-calm.
  • Numerics: enable tabular figures for tables, counts, dates, points.

Reusable elements observed (a starting component list)

  • Stepper (5-node horizontal, icon + label; active = brand red).
  • Selectable option cards (Target/Trigger/Benefit choices) — needs the new selection state.
  • Live summary rail ("Offer Summary") — a signature component; elevate it.
  • Pill toggle (Free / Amount / Percentage).
  • Inline expanding sub-forms (criteria/unit/group rows) — needs breathing room + labelled controls.
  • Dropdowns, number steppers, date pickers, rich-text editor, image upload, "Generate with AI" button.
  • Dense data tables (campaigns list) + modal (segment breakdown with distribution bars) — reusable analytics patterns.
  • Left nav (grouped, collapsible) — restructure + rename in plain language.

Accessibility guardrails

  • Don't rely on red alone to signal state (colour-blind users + the selection/error confusion). Pair colour with icon, border weight, and text.
  • Contrast: body text ≥ 4.5:1 on white; brand red on white passes for large text but verify red-on-red and white-on-red combos (LOD uses white text on red buttons — fine at button size; avoid red text on light-pink fills).
  • Target sizes ≥ 40px for the primarily-mouse enterprise users; keyboard-navigable stepper and forms.
  • Plain language over jargon (an accessibility and comprehension win for non-technical marketers): rename "C/V Definitions", "Award Rule", etc. where possible.

Brand voice (for microcopy)

Confident, plain, helpful. The tool should sound like a calm expert, not a technical manual. The existing step headings already model this well — "Choose your target audience for maximum impact," "Define what customers receive when they complete the action." Keep that voice; extend it to labels, empty states, and validation ("Add at least one product group to continue" beats a bare red border).
